newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian bombs may affect democracy plan.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian bombs may affect democracy plan.

text.p: A wave of bomb blasts in Nigeria's biggest city Lagos has spread panic in Africa's most populous nation and could affect the military government's programme to restore democracy next year.

Shunned by the West over its human rights record and lack of democracy, General Sani Abacha's government last year began implementing a plan to hand over to an elected president in October 1998 which critics dismiss as a ruse to stay in power.

But the government has repeatedly stressed that it would go ahead with the programme and on Thursday announced new dates for registration of voters and local council polls in March to precede more serious state and federal polls in 1997 and 1998.
"It is arguable whether terrorism can easily bring about an end to military dictatorship," wrote political commentator Bola Akinterinwa in the independent Thisday newspaper on Saturday.

"In fact, the destabilisation can, at best, prevent the military from focusing more seriously on the transition programme...By implication, therefore, the military will have a powerful and of course a legitimate excuse to stay beyond 1998," he added.
Three bomb attacks clearly targeting the military have gone off since December killing at least three soldiers and wounding several dozens.

British Broadcasting Corporation radio reported that a previously unknown group calling itself Liberation Organisation of Nigeria claimed responsibility for the latest explosion last Tuesday near Albati barracks in the heart of Lagos.

The group had not been heard of before and its demands are not known but the government blames the exiled opposition, which it says is linked to the umbrella NADECO opposition group at home, for the bomb blasts.

NADECO fears the government could use the attacks to rope in government opponents and has pointed to the detention in Lagos since Thursday of former finance minister Olu Falae, a member of the NADECO group, as the beginning of another clampdown.
Western diplomats said the attacks could add to the pressure on Nigeria's government to negotiate with the opposition but doubted that this would happen.

"The positions on both sides are strongly entrenched and it is not certain whether the government will bow to it," said one diplomat who has followed the crisis in Nigeria since 1993 when the army annulled a presidential poll to restore democracy.
Abacha seized power in the chaos of that year.

While he has subdued the strikes and riots which gripped Lagos and the southwest, the home region of Moshood Abiola, the wealthy businessman presumed to have won the 1993 vote, his relations with the West have been strained over human rights and the slow pace of democratisation.
Abiola has remained in detention since 1994 when he proclaimed himself president in defiance of the military.
Pressure for him and other detained opponents to be freed has yielded little as only a few have been released.
Nigeria vehemently rejects such pressures from abroad as interference in its internal affairs.
According to Information Minister Walter Ofonagoro, unnamed Western nations are behind the Lagos bombings with the intention of putting pressure on the government.
"They are trying to push the government to declare a state of emergency but the government won't," he told reporters in the capital Abuja on Thursday.
Many residents of Lagos, a sprawling city of six million people, have been scared by the bombs and wonder for long the attacks will go on.
Many Nigerians fear that if the situation degenerates then a state of emergency would be on the cards.
Others say negotiations with the opposition would avert further anarchy.

"The option we have is to sit down and dialogue. NADECO is not made of foreigners," a former interior minister, retired Major-General Mohammed Magaro, told reporters in Kaduna, northern Nigeria on Friday.
